title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: Historians assume that great men lead humanity toward certain goals: the greatness of Russia or of France, the balance of power in Europe, the spread of the ideas of the Revolution, general progress, or anything else. If we make that same assumption, there's no way to explain the facts of history without bringing in the ideas of chance and genius.

If the goal of the European wars at the start of the nineteenth century had been the aggrandizement of Russia, that goal could have been reached without all the wars that came before it, and without the invasion. If the goal was the aggrandizement of France, that could have been reached without the Revolution and without the Empire. If the goal was spreading ideas, the printing press could have done that job far better than warfare. If the goal was the progress of civilization, it's easy enough to see that there are other, more expedient ways of spreading civilization than by destroying wealth and human lives.
Why did it happen this way, and not some other way?
Because that's how it happened! "Chance created the situation; genius made use of it," says history.
But what is chance? What is genius?

The words "chance" and "genius" don't point to any real, existing thing, and so they can't be defined. They only mark a certain stage in our understanding of phenomena. I don't know why some particular event happens; I think I can't know it; so I do not try to know it, and I call it chance. I see a force producing effects that go beyond the reach of ordinary human power; I don't understand why this is happening, and I call it genius.

To a flock of rams, the one ram that the shepherd drives every evening into a separate pen to be fed, and that grows twice as fat as the rest, must look like a genius. And it must seem an astonishing coincidence of genius with a whole run of extraordinary chances that this particular ram—the one that, instead of going into the general fold every evening, goes into a special pen full of oats—that this very ram, now bursting with fat, ends up slaughtered for meat.

But all the rams would have to do is stop assuming that everything that happens to them happens purely for the sake of their sheepish goals; they'd only have to admit that whatever happens to them might also have purposes beyond their understanding, and right away they'd see a unity, a coherence, in everything that happened to that fattened ram. Even without knowing what purpose they were being fattened for, they would at least know that nothing that happened to the ram happened by accident, and they would no longer need the ideas of chance or genius.

We have to give up our claim to make out some purpose we can immediately grasp, and admit that the ultimate purpose lies beyond our understanding. Only then can we see the sequence running through the experiences of historical figures, and grasp the cause behind the effects they produce—effects out of all proportion to ordinary human capacities. And once we do that, the words "chance" and "genius" become unnecessary.

We need only admit that we don't know the purpose behind the European convulsions. All we know are the facts: the murders, first in France, then in Italy, in Africa, in Prussia, in Austria, in Spain, and in Russia. And we need only admit that the movements from west to east and from east to west form the essence and the point of these events. Once we admit that, we won't just have no need to see extraordinary ability and genius in Napoleon and Alexander—we'll be unable to see them as anything but men like other men. And we won't need to reach for chance to explain the small events that made these men what they were, but it will be plain that every one of those small events was inevitable.

By giving up any claim to know the ultimate purpose, we'll see clearly that no one could imagine a blossom or a seed better suited to any given plant than the ones it produces. In just the same way, it's impossible to imagine any two people more perfectly fitted, down to the smallest detail, for the purpose they had to fulfill, than Napoleon and Alexander, with all their antecedents.
